questions.stem: A boat is floating on the sea as waves pass beneath it. Which statement best describes the motion of the boat?

options.text: The boat moves forward with the wave
The boat moves up and down but stays in roughly the same position
The boat is pushed towards the shore by the wave energy
The boat moves in the same direction as the wave speed

questions.explanation: Waves transfer energy, not matter. The boat (like all objects on waves) oscillates up and down but does not travel with the wave. Options A, C, and D incorrectly suggest the boat is carried along — this is a common misconception because waves appear to move water forward, but the water particles (and the boat) only oscillate about a fixed position.

questions.stem: A wave has a frequency of 5 Hz and a wavelength of 2 m. What is the speed of the wave?
questions.explanation: Using v = f x wavelength: v = 5 Hz x 2 m = 10 m/s. Option A (2.5) comes from dividing frequency by wavelength, option C (7) from adding them — both are common arithmetic errors. The correct relationship is multiplication.

questions.stem: A student observes a wave on an oscilloscope. The distance from the rest position to the top of the wave is 3 cm, and the distance from crest to trough is 6 cm. What is the amplitude of the wave?
questions.explanation: Amplitude is the maximum displacement from the rest (equilibrium) position, which is 3 cm. A common mistake is to measure from crest to trough (6 cm, option A), but that is twice the amplitude. The amplitude is always measured from the rest position to the peak, not from peak to trough.

questions.stem: A surfer notices that 12 wave crests pass a fixed point in 60 seconds. What is the frequency of the waves?
questions.explanation: Frequency = number of waves / time = 12 / 60 = 0.2 Hz. Option C (5) comes from dividing 60/12 (giving the period, not the frequency). Option D confuses the count of waves with the frequency. Frequency is how many complete waves pass per second.

questions.stem: Two waves have the same frequency. Wave A has double the amplitude of Wave B. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Wave A transfers twice as much energy as Wave B
Wave A has double the wavelength of Wave B
Wave A transfers more energy than Wave B
Both waves transfer the same amount of energy

questions.explanation: A wave with a larger amplitude transfers more energy. Option A is tempting but the energy carried by a wave is proportional to the square of the amplitude, not directly proportional — so double the amplitude means four times the energy, not twice. Option B is wrong because amplitude and wavelength are independent properties. Option D is wrong because amplitude directly affects energy transfer.
